criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1. This three-essay environmental economics dissertation examines behavioral decisions related to water quality problems rather than household or community water or sanitation service access. Manuscript 1 studies recreational visitation to coastal saltwater beaches in Southern New England. Manuscripts 2 and 3 study US adults' perceptions of PFAS drinking-water contamination and household adoption/purchase of commercial point-of-use PFAS-removing water filters (averting behavior among households that already have tap water from public systems or private wells), not water or sanitation utility connection, service access, continuity, or disconnection.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails Criterion 2 under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and would still be excluded overall even if viewed leniently under the plain wording. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, none of the three essays examines a legal or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure governing access): Manuscript 1 models biophysical satellite water clarity and bacterial beach closure notifications on coastal beach recreation (mentioning historical redlining and beach parking/shoreline access only as narrative context in the Discussion); Manuscript 2 examines psychological behavior-change constructs (HBM, TPB, TTM), organoleptic water perceptions, subjective survey ratings of awareness of and confidence in PFAS regulations, and a descriptive indicator for private well vs. public water system (treating historical regulatory exclusion of private wells as background context); and Manuscript 3 tests generic vs. personalized PFAS risk-information infographics (behavioural promotion/nudges, explicitly outside narrow Criterion 2). Under the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, beach closure notifications (M1) and subjective awareness/confidence in PFAS regulations or private-well regulatory coverage (M2) touch tangentially on regulatory factors, though not as institutional determinants of water/sanitation service access; even if treated as passing plain Criterion 2, the record still fails Criteria 1 and 4, so plain_criterion2_decision is exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies Criterion 3. All three dissertation chapters report original quantitative empirical analyses: Manuscript 1 estimates a multiple-site zonal travel cost model combining anonymized cell phone mobility data, Landsat 8 water clarity, BEACON beach closure data, and US Census block group data (40,345 to 41,473 CBG-POI-month observations); Manuscript 2 analyzes a nationally representative Prolific online survey of 1,935 US adults using polychoric correlations, LASSO variable selection, and logistic regressions; and Manuscript 3 conducts an online randomized controlled trial among 1,603 non-filter-owning survey participants.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4. Reported outcomes are recreational beach visitation per capita and recreational consumer surplus (Manuscript 1), self-reported PFAS knowledge/awareness/concern and ownership of a point-of-use PFAS-removing water filter (Manuscript 2), and online filter-link clicks, willingness to pay, purchase intention, and proof of point-of-use water filter purchase (Manuscript 3). None of these measures household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, continuity, quantity, utility affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Satisfies Criterion 5. Units of analysis, populations, exposures/treatments, outcomes, and study designs are clearly identifiable across all three essays from the provided text (Manuscript 1 at the Census Block Group-Point of Interest-month level; Manuscripts 2 and 3 at the individual/household respondent level in a nationally representative US online survey and embedded RCT; although the PDF text is truncated after page 117 before Manuscript 3's body, Manuscript 3's exact RCT design, sample sizes, treatments, and outcomes are fully specified in the Dissertation Abstract and List of Tables/Figures).
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies Criterion 6. The dissertation is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: Hence, this dissertation addresses these challenges through three empirical studies. The first chapter evaluates the effect of water quality on recreational beach use and its heterogenous impact across racial and income groups. The second investigates national patterns in knowledge, awareness, and concern about PFAS pollution and the drivers of current adoption of water filters. The third assesses whether personalized risk information can motivate self-protective behaviors.

We applied the data in a multiple-site zonal travel cost model to estimate the effect of water quality on recreational beach choice and compute welfare distribution across different income and racial groups for a 10% improvement in water clarity.

Drawing on a survey of 1,935 nationally representative US adults, this study investigates national patterns in knowledge, awareness, and concern about PFAS pollution and their associations with the adoption of PFAS-removing water filters.

To study household responses to PFAS contamination, we fielded a nationally representative online survey and conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) targeting 2000 people. The survey assessed water preferences, self-assessed PFAS knowledge and risk, water supply type (private well vs. public), and socio-demographic characteristics.

The RCT tested the impact of three information treatments: none, generic, and personalized PFAS information. Personalized PFAS information had three messages tailored to specific household vulnerabilities, such as the presence of children, pregnancy, or PFAS-related diseases. We then compared search behavior, stated interest, and actual proof of water filter purchases across treatment groups.

raw_response.exposure: Manuscript 1: Coastal satellite water clarity, bacterial beach closure events (BCEs), and action duration days (ADDs) interacted with Census Block Group poverty/disadvantaged status and racial composition. Manuscript 2: Tap water taste/color satisfaction, water supply type (private well vs. public system), sociodemographics, and self-reported PFAS knowledge, regulatory awareness/confidence, and concern. Manuscript 3: Randomized online information treatments (no information control, generic PFAS infographic, personalized PFAS vulnerability infographic).
raw_response.outcome: Manuscript 1: Monthly recreational saltwater beach visits per capita (ln visits per capita from CBG to POI) and recreational consumer surplus. Manuscript 2: Self-reported PFAS knowledge, awareness, and concern, and binary household ownership of a PFAS-removing water filter. Manuscript 3: Submission of valid proof of water filter purchase, willingness to pay for a certified PFAS filter, purchase intention, and clicks on external water-filter information links.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Manuscript 1: Rhode Island Census Block Groups visiting 789 coastal beach Points of Interest within 100 miles of the RI border in summer 2018-2019 (40,345 to 41,473 CBG-POI-month observations). Manuscript 2: Nationally representative Prolific online sample of US adults aged 18+ (N = 1,935). Manuscript 3: Subset of survey participants not owning a PFAS-removing water filter randomized into Control (N = 623), Treatment 1 (N = 627), and Treatment 2 (N = 353) (total N = 1,603).
raw_response.rationale: Exclude under E01 (Wrong topic — water-quality behavioral economics study without household/community water or sanitation service access or a rule-type access governance mechanism, per Exclusion Criteria 3 and 7). Across its three empirical essays, this 2025 PhD dissertation examines (1) coastal saltwater beach recreational visitation in response to water clarity and bacterial beach closures in Southern New England, (2) US adults' subjective knowledge, regulatory awareness/confidence, sensory perceptions, and ownership of point-of-use PFAS-removing water filters, and (3) an online RCT testing generic and personalized PFAS risk-information nudges on commercial water filter purchases. None of the chapters examines household or community access to water or sanitation utility services (c1=no, c4=no) or a legal/administrative rule-type mechanism governing service access (c2=no).
raw_response.study_design: Three-essay quantitative empirical dissertation: (1) observational panel multiple-site zonal travel cost model using cell phone mobility and remote-sensing data; (2) cross-sectional nationally representative online survey with polychoric correlation, LASSO, and logistic regression; (3) online randomized controlled trial (RCT).
